section_summary: This section documents Allied efforts in late 1941 to restrict Japan’s access to strategic commodities, including mercury, cotton, nickel, iron ore, petroleum products, and Brazilian minerals. It contains diplomatic telegrams and despatches about Japanese purchasing and shipping in Latin America, policy memoranda on preclusive buying and export controls, and manifests for the Japanese vessel Toa Maru. The final documents concern Japanese financial channels and transactions by blocked firms in Bolivia.

subfiles.title: Continuation of despatch on contraband mercury at Tampico
subfiles.from: Henry A. Hoyt, American Vice Consul
subfiles.about: Reports additional contraband mercury found in an embargoed railway car at Tampico.
subfiles.summary: Hoyt: a car embargoed at Tampico held considerable mercury; he believes the same people were behind an earlier contraband case, and notes distribution of the report.

subfiles.title: Recent purchasing activities in Brazil of Japanese agents
subfiles.from: John F. Simmons, for the American Ambassador at Rio de Janeiro
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese agents’ efforts to purchase Brazilian rock crystal for the Japanese Navy.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy reports that Hiroshi Yoda and Yoshio Kobayashi arrived in Brazil in August as purchasing agents for the Japanese Navy. They allegedly planned to turn quartz crystal into small images to evade export restrictions, prompting the Embassy to ask the Bank of Brazil to prohibit the exports.

subfiles.title: Telegram from Asunción concerning shipment manifests
subfiles.about: Relays a Buenos Aires report that no relevant shipments appeared on manifests.
subfiles.summary: Asuncion telegram citing an October 21 message: Buenos Aires found no shipments manifested, apparently on exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: Shipments of mercury from Spain to Japan via Argentina
subfiles.about: Explains British policy and updated intelligence concerning Spanish mercury shipments routed through Argentina to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Britain can't legally stop neutral shipments to Japan without evidence of enemy benefit but will obstruct Spanish and Portuguese strategic exports administratively; 5,000 flasks shipped in August arrived on the Aldecoa and Mar Cantabrico, and the British ambassador invites U.S. proposals.

subfiles.title: Telegram on Argentine cotton exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports that Argentina had exported no cotton to Japan since August.
subfiles.summary: Armour: statistics and trade information show no Argentine cotton exports to Japan since August, answering the October 18 inquiry.

subfiles.title: Telegram on Paraguayan cotton shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports that shipping manifests show no Paraguayan cotton sent to Japan since August 1.
subfiles.summary: Embassy examined shipping manifests and found no Paraguayan cotton shipped to Japan after August 1, 1941.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 1243 on Spanish mercury in Argentina
subfiles.from: Norman Armour, American Embassy at Buenos Aires
subfiles.about: Corrects the report that additional Spanish mercury remained in Argentina awaiting shipment to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 1243: British information on mercury held in Argentina for Japan was wrong; only 5,000 flasks arrived and all left in August; Argentine law apparently doesn't allow seizing transshipments. Page 411 paraphrases it.

subfiles.title: Letter transmitting cotton statistics
subfiles.to: Jacques J. Reinstein, Department of State
subfiles.about: Transmits the cotton figures Dent had shown Reinstein earlier that day.
subfiles.summary: Dent encloses cotton supply and trade statistics, delivered by safe hand to the Commercial Treaties and Agreements Division.

subfiles.title: Cotton supply, exports, stocks, and prospective surpluses
subfiles.about: Compiles historical and projected cotton production, trade, stocks, consumption, and exportable surpluses.
subfiles.summary: The tables compare United States and Indian cotton exports, Japanese imports and production, wartime stocks, and anticipated 1941–42 supplies. They estimate substantial exportable surpluses in the United States, India, and the Western Hemisphere and discuss Brazil, Peru, Argentina, Mexico, and Paraguay. A supplementary note adds Burmese figures, and the closing pages list statistical sources.

subfiles.title: Exports of nickel from New Caledonia
subfiles.doc_type: memorandum of conversation with duplicate copies
subfiles.about: Records John Dent’s explanation of the practical restriction on nickel exports from New Caledonia to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Dent says no formal embargo exists, but New Caledonian nickel ore must be sold to a smelter limiting sales to Australia and New Zealand, so Britain sees no need to press the Free French; four pages are copies.

subfiles.title: Exports of iron ore from the Philippines to Japan
subfiles.doc_type: memorandum of conversation with duplicate copy
subfiles.about: Clarifies the status of Philippine iron-ore quotas and licenses after a British inquiry.
subfiles.summary: Dent asks whether Britain should stop 20,000 tons of Malayan ore monthly to Japan; Reinstein says Philippine licenses for about 160,000 tons remain but nothing sailed since August 7, and new applications are held in Washington. Pages 427-428 duplicate 425-426.

subfiles.title: Source of the Reuters oil-embargo report
subfiles.about: Reports that a Reuters dispatch about a three-power oil embargo originated with an Associated Press story.
subfiles.summary: Baron van Boetzelaer says Reuters' New York office based its East Indies message about an oil embargo on the Associated Press Washington report.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Baron van Boetzelaer about oil shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Records a Netherlands inquiry concerning a press report that three governments had agreed to stop all oil shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Van Boetzelaer asks about a Washington Post report that the U.S., Britain and the Dutch agreed to halt all oil to Japan; Hiss knows of no further basis and will consult superiors.

subfiles.title: “3 Nations Act to Stop All Oil to Japan”
subfiles.about: Reports an alleged agreement by the United States, Great Britain, and the Netherlands to halt oil shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Damaged clipping "3 Nations Act to Stop All Oil to Japan" claims agreement after the July freeze and discusses limited oil for the Tatuta Maru.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Nisiyama concerning payment for oil and the Yokohama Specie Bank
subfiles.to: Department of State and Treasury files
subfiles.about: Records discussions of Japanese proposals to pay for American oil and the liquidity of the Yokohama Specie Bank’s New York agency.
subfiles.summary: Nisiyama says Japan will pay for pending oil with South American balances via Banco do Brasil and Chase; Pehle questions how they became available and raises Yokohama Specie Bank withdrawals, and they discuss missionary remittances.

subfiles.title: Japanese memorandum on financing pending oil purchases
subfiles.about: Outlines a proposed use of Japanese funds in South America to pay American oil suppliers.
subfiles.summary: The badly degraded text refers to the delay in receiving an answer to proposals involving gold or dollar currency from Japan. It describes using funds handled through the Banco do Brasil and New York banks to make payments connected with Mitsui and American oil interests, including Richfield.

subfiles.title: Letter forwarding survey of preclusive cotton buying
subfiles.from: L. Wheeler, United States Department of Agriculture
subfiles.about: Forwards a memorandum on preclusive buying of Latin American cotton for Economic Defense Board discussion.
subfiles.summary: Wheeler sends his office's survey of preclusive cotton buying per an October 8 committee decision, due for next Friday's meeting.

subfiles.title: Preclusive buying of Latin American cotton: A preliminary survey
subfiles.about: Assesses the feasibility and cost of buying Latin American cotton to deny it to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The survey estimates that more than three million bales of Latin American cotton could be bought by the United States and United Kingdom for roughly $120 million. It concludes that Japan could survive for over two years using stocks, curtailed consumption, and Chinese cotton, but preclusive purchases would impede Japanese textile exports and assist producers in Brazil and Peru. The attached table estimates stocks, crops, domestic use, and exportable surpluses throughout the world.

subfiles.title: British Embassy letter concerning castor oil in Brazil
subfiles.about: Provides British information concerning castor oil in Brazil.
subfiles.summary: Mostly illegible British Embassy letter on Brazilian castor oil.

subfiles.title: Letter forwarding British information on Brazilian castor oil
subfiles.to: D. A. Fitzgerald, Department of Agriculture
subfiles.about: Forwards the British Embassy’s October 14 letter about castor oil in Brazil.
subfiles.summary: Finletter sends Fitzgerald the British Embassy letter on Brazilian castor oil, possibly of interest to Agriculture.

subfiles.title: Memorandum for Collado on cotton movements and immobilized shipping
subfiles.about: Lists information requested by Milo Perkins concerning cotton shipments, immobilized vessels, and possible gasoline reexports.
subfiles.summary: Acheson asks Collado for cotton movements since August 1 to Japan and China, a status report on immobilized ships and whether a State representative in South America would help; he adds Perkins's inquiry on U.S. gasoline reaching Germany via Spain.

subfiles.title: Memorandum to Bunn on gasoline exports to Spain
subfiles.about: Requests completion of a policy review prompted by an unverified report that gasoline sent to Spain was reexported to Germany.
subfiles.summary: Acheson tells Bunn the Spain gasoline report came from a sailor and wasn't reliable enough to change policy, and asks whether the Stinebower, Reinstein and George committee wrote a policy statement.

subfiles.title: Letter transmitting cotton statistics for China and Manchukuo
subfiles.about: Transmits statistical material for China and Manchukuo supplementary to cotton figures for Peru and Brazil.
subfiles.summary: Dent refers to another letter on Peruvian and Brazilian cotton and encloses new British Embassy figures for China and Manchukuo.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of cotton statistics
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of Dent’s letter and cotton statistics.
subfiles.summary: Reinstein thanks Dent for the October 1 letter. The acknowledgment describes the enclosure as statistics on Peruvian and Brazilian cotton.

subfiles.title: Memorandum recommending deferral of a telegram to Mexico
subfiles.to: Dean Acheson and the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Recommends delaying a proposed request to Mexico pending the outcome of broader negotiations.
subfiles.summary: Duggan advises that the Department wait two or three days for clarification of the general Mexican negotiations. He believes Mexico will comply with the attached request if the broader agreements proceed, making immediate dispatch of the telegram undesirable.

subfiles.title: Telegram on proposed Mexican cotton exports to Japan
subfiles.from: F. McGurk, American Embassy in Mexico City
subfiles.about: Reports a Mexican company’s plan to export 10,000–20,000 bales of cotton to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Algodonera Figueroa asked the Embassy's view of a proposed Mexican cotton sale to Japan; McGurk says a word to the Foreign Minister would probably stop it and requests instructions.

subfiles.title: Instruction to oppose Mexican cotton exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Directs the Embassy to ask Mexico to prevent the proposed cotton shipment to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Embassy is told to say Washington wants Mexican cotton exports to Japan stopped, confidentially noting the U.S. blocks its own; the Department prefers case-by-case handling to avoid counterproductive publicity.

subfiles.title: Instruction to investigate stopping the Howell Lykes shipment
subfiles.about: Asks what action could stop a shipment, including possible cancellation of the vessel’s charter.
subfiles.summary: Carr says Acheson wants Hiss to find what could halt the Howell Lykes shipment, including whether the Maritime Commission could cancel the charter.

subfiles.title: Customs memorandum on lubricating oil aboard the Howell Lykes
subfiles.from: W. R. Johnson, Commissioner of Customs
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Green, Division of Controls
subfiles.about: Reports a large shipment of lubricating oil from New Orleans to Mitsui Bussan Kaisha in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Customs reports that Phillips Petroleum filed an export declaration for 30,514 wooden barrels of lubricating oil valued at $336,418. The oil was consigned to Mitsui Bussan Kaisha at Moji and scheduled for shipment on the American SS Howell Lykes. Page 458 is a duplicate copy with OCR errors.

subfiles.title: Instruction to investigate petrolatum carried by the Heiyo Maru
subfiles.to: American Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, Mexico City
subfiles.about: Orders a discreet investigation of American-origin petrolatum allegedly reexported from Mexico to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Airmail instruction: the Heiyo Maru left Manzanillo for Yokohama with 250 drums of Snow White Petrolatum consigned by A. Z. Phillips, bought via Petroleos Mexicanos; the Chargé is to investigate.

subfiles.title: Shipment of Snow White Petrolatum to Yokohama
subfiles.from: Josephus Daniels, American Ambassador to Mexico
subfiles.about: Reports the investigation of petrolatum ordered by A. Z. Phillips and possibly carried on the Heiyo Maru.
subfiles.summary: Phillips ordered 500 drums via Petroleos Mexicanos; police opened the car but found one drum and lost the rest; the Heiyo Maru manifest listed other Phillips cargo, and an FBI source saw 400 drums aboard. Pages 462-463 duplicate.

subfiles.title: Further despatch on A. Z. Phillips’s petrolatum shipment
subfiles.from: F. McGurk, Chargé d’Affaires ad interim
subfiles.about: Forwards an intercepted message mentioning Phillips’s petrolatum and other strategic-material transactions.
subfiles.summary: McGurk supplements the November 7 report on Phillips's petrolatum, enclosing an FBI attaché Gus Jones message on it and other transactions.

subfiles.title: Intercepted radiogram from Mexico City to Japan
subfiles.from: A. Z. Phillips or associates in Mexico City
subfiles.about: Discusses copper, mercury, drums, petroleum, payments, and the planned reshipment of Snow White Petrolatum to Manzanillo.
subfiles.summary: Intercepted Mexico City radiogram offers copper and 1,000 flasks of mercury, seeks 8,000 empty drums and a gasoline tanker, says Phillips owned a million barrels of Poza Rica crude, and urges settling Mitsubishi accounts via New York.

subfiles.title: Memorandum concerning a reply to Marvin R. Schafer
subfiles.about: Refers one of Schafer’s questions for reply and proposes language explaining American policy toward the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: Suggests answering Marvin Schafer by enclosing Welles's June 23 statement: aid to forces opposing Hitlerism is distinct from judging the Soviet regime.

subfiles.title: Japanese-Brazilian trade and the voyage of the Toa Maru
subfiles.from: John F. Simmons, for the American Ambassador at Rio de Janeiro
subfiles.about: Assesses the Toa Maru’s cargo as evidence of the strengths and gaps in American preclusive purchasing in Brazil.
subfiles.summary: The Toa Maru, first Japanese ship in a Brazilian port since August, sailed November 1 via Buenos Aires with no agreement commodities but many armament materials; Simmons warns Japan may later seek Brazilian materials via West Coast transshipment.

subfiles.title: Outward manifest of the Toa Maru
subfiles.about: Lists Brazilian exports carried by the Toa Maru to Osaka and Yokohama.
subfiles.summary: Toa Maru outward manifest: quebracho extract, monazite, pig iron, fluorspar, wolfram, cobalt ore, graphite, carnauba wax, tantalite, gum, drugs and ipecac, not yet covered by preclusive agreements.

subfiles.title: Inward manifest of the Toa Maru
subfiles.about: Lists cargo brought into Brazil by the Toa Maru from Asian, Australian, and Chilean ports.
subfiles.summary: The manifest records cargo from Kobe, Tientsin, Shanghai, Hong Kong, Sydney, Nagoya, Yokohama, and Valparaíso. Goods included electrical equipment, personal effects, chemicals, foodstuffs, porcelain, celluloid products, raw silk, silk yarn, transformers, generators, cable, and motors. It identifies consignors, consignees, quantities, and weights.

subfiles.title: Handwritten analysis of strategic cargo exported on the Toa Maru
subfiles.to: Special Assistant to the Secretary’s office
subfiles.about: Reviews whether the principal commodities on the Toa Maru were covered by the strategic-materials agreement with Brazil.
subfiles.summary: Handwritten analysis: pig iron and fluorspar were outside the agreement, wolfram and cobalt not yet included, graphite shipped once, tantalite needs action, carnauba wax needs checking; no iron ore went, as Britain wanted it left for its purchases.

subfiles.title: Memorandum requesting review of Toa Maru commodities
subfiles.from: Thomas K. Finletter, Division of Defense Materials
subfiles.about: Requests a commodity-by-commodity review of the Toa Maru’s Brazilian exports.
subfiles.summary: Finletter asks whether the Toa Maru's monazite, pig iron, fluorspar, wolfram, cobalt and graphite were covered by the Brazil agreement, and urges faster action on carnauba wax, tantalite and ipecac.

subfiles.title: Transmittal to the Treasury concerning Japanese financial transactions in Bolivia
subfiles.about: Forwards the La Paz Legation’s report on transactions involving Japanese and blocked firms in Bolivia.
subfiles.summary: Secretary sends Treasury despatch 1297 on financial transactions by Japanese and Proclaimed List firms in Bolivia.

subfiles.title: Financial transactions by Japanese and German firms in Bolivia
subfiles.from: Allan Dawson, Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, La Paz
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese remittance arrangements and dollar-draft purchases by blocked or front firms in Bolivia.
subfiles.summary: Dawson reports Japanese collections in Bolivia routed via Lima banks for the Yokohama Specie Bank, details dollar drafts bought by A. Siles, Kyllmann Bauer and other blocked interests, and suspects some American firms knowingly dealt with listed firms.
